title: HCI Module 7 — Usability Testing, UAT and Interface Testing
description: Exam revision: usability, ISO 9241-11, goals of usability testing, formal vs informal tests, the 5-step process, best practices, pros/cons, User Acceptance Testing, V-model and interface testing.
endCard: 📘 Usability Testing — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: Watch real users — find the problems before launch

lines: You built it, and it works. But can real people actually use it?
That's what usability testing finds out.
We'll cover usability, its goals, the five step testing process, best practices, user acceptance testing, and interface testing.

scenes.title: 1. Why it matters for V & V

items.b: usability is an important attribute of good quality software
quality software meets the user's needs
software easy to understand, learn and use
usable software increases user productivity and satisfaction

lines: Why is usability part of verification and validation? Because usability is an important attribute of good quality software.
Quality software is software that meets the user's needs.
Those needs may require software that's easy to understand, learn, and use.
And usable software increases user productivity and user satisfaction.

scenes.title: 2. Know your goal

rows.t: goal: identify the problem areas of your software / Web site by testing, to solve those problems
and always keep your tests and analysis simple!

lines: The important point to remember: know your goal. Identify the problem areas of your software or web site by testing, so you can solve them.
And always keep your tests and analysis simple.

scenes.title: 3. What is usability? (ISO 9241-11)

items.b: a measure of how easy it is to use something — understand, learn, operate · “user-friendliness”
…can be used by specified users
…to achieve specified goals
can they achieve the goal?
with how little effort / time?
…in a specified context of use

viz.note: ISO 9241-11 → E E S: Effectiveness, Efficiency, Satisfaction

lines: Usability is a measure of how easy it is to use something: how easily a typical user can understand, learn and operate the software. In short, user friendliness.
The ISO definition, nine two four one dash eleven: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals,
with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction, in a specified context of use.
Remember E, E, S: effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction.

scenes.title: 4. What is usability testing?

items.b: ascertain the degree to which software meets the usability needs of its intended users — difficult to evaluate & measure
needed to learn the software
to become efficient using it
measured increase in user productivity
subjective assessment of the user's attitude
place users in front of a version of the software and watch them
can be expensive · not cost-effective if done too late
uncovers problems that guidelines & inspections missed

lines: Usability testing tries to ascertain the degree to which software meets the usability needs of its intended users. And usability is difficult to evaluate and measure.
It tries to quantify user friendliness by four measures:
the skill needed to learn the software, the time to become efficient, the measured increase in productivity, and a subjective assessment of the user's attitude.
The idea: place users in front of some version of the software, and watch how they try to use it.
It can be expensive, depending on the tasks and what you watch for, and it's not cost effective if done too late in development.
But it can uncover usability problems that design guidelines and inspections may have missed.

scenes.title: 5. Goals — is the application…
lines: Usability testing determines whether an application is
useful, findable, accessible, usable,
and desirable.
Memory hook: Users Find Apps Useful Daily.

scenes.title: 6. Parameters tested

items.b: easy to learn? · useful, adds value? · content, colour, icons, images aesthetically pleasing?
minimal navigation to reach a screen · scroll bars not used often · uniform page format · search provided
no outdated or incorrect data (contact info, address) · no broken links
self-explanatory controls, no training needed · help provided

lines: The goal is to satisfy users, by checking four parameters of the system.
Effectiveness: is it easy to learn, is it useful and does it add value, and are the content, colours, icons and images aesthetically pleasing?
Efficiency: very little navigation to reach a screen, scroll bars not used frequently, a uniform format across pages, and a way to search.
Accuracy: no outdated or incorrect data like contact details or addresses, and no broken links.
User friendliness: self explanatory controls that need no training, and help for users. Aligning with these goals makes testing effective.

scenes.title: 7. Formal vs informal testing

items.b:
build a usability lab: computers, audio-video equipment
staffed by psychologists, technicians and HCI specialists

no fancy lab — simple test plan + task list, notepad and pencil
observed by an impartial moderator
✔ shows what people really do, in real work, in an ordinary setting

lines: Formal testing might mean building a usability lab, with computers and audio video equipment, staffed by psychologists, technicians and HCI specialists.
The informal approach needs no fancy lab: a simple test plan and task list, a notepad and pencil, and an impartial moderator observing.
Its advantage: it shows what people actually do, doing real work, in an ordinary setting.

scenes.title: 8. The 5-step process
lines: Testing basics follow a five step process.
Plan and prepare. Find participants. Conduct the tests. Analyze results. Make recommendations.
Memory hook: plan, people, perform, ponder, propose.

scenes.title: 9. Step 1 — Plan & prepare

items.b:
simple test → list of questions
detailed test → prepared script
creates a framework · communicates goals to the client, aligns expectations

tasks a typical user can finish in an hour · not too simple, not too hard
e.g. 1 find a concert · 2 buy tickets online · 3 find directions to venue
pencil, paper, computer, browser · maybe a video camera · dev team may watch · user's own environment · printed site for notes

lines: Step one: plan and prepare. Develop a test plan: a list of questions for simple testing, or a prepared script for detailed testing.
The plan creates a framework for testing, and lets you communicate goals with the client and align expectations.
Create a task list that a typical user can complete in an hour. Not too simple, not too difficult.
For example: find a concert you want to see, purchase tickets online, and find directions to the venue.
Informal tests need only pencil, paper, a computer and browser. Sometimes a video camera records sessions, or the dev team watches.
Tests can run in the user's own environment. Keep a printed version of the site for notes, then watch and learn.

scenes.title: 10. Step 2 — Find participants

items.b: finding suitable participants is a challenging aspect
gather an ongoing base of users
people not associated with your company or Web site
try the plan on co-workers / friends with Web experience · first test: fun, informative, low-stress

lines: Step two: find participants. This is one of the most challenging parts of usability testing.
It's important to gather an ongoing user base.
Test outside the team, with people not associated with your company or your web site.
Before real sessions, try your test plan on co-workers or friends with decent web experience. The first test should be fun, informative and low stress.

scenes.title: 11. Step 3 — Conduct the session

nodes.b: introduce yourself, explain the process
don't tell them how many tasks or how long each takes

nodes.h: Speak only to give a new task
nodes.b: take notes during the process
specific problem areas · unexpected results · personal observations

lines: Step three: conduct the session. Introduce yourself and explain the process to the user.
The user performs a set of pre-defined tasks, but don't tell them how many, or how long each will take.
Make the user feel comfortable. Speak only to give a new task, and take notes during the process.
When the session is over, prepare a short summary of the session and results: specific problem areas, unexpected results, and your personal observations.

scenes.title: 12. Collect basic data + post-test survey

items.b: could the user complete the task?
problems / obstacles
overall commentary
let the user speak their mind
online or paper · graphics, logic, content, navigation, overall satisfaction
of the site vs. the goal of each task

lines: Collect basic data. Could the user complete the task? Did they need help? How much time did it take?
Note any stumbling blocks, and your overall observations and commentary.
Debrief the user, and let them speak their mind.
Then the post-test survey, online or on paper: what they thought of the graphics, logic, content, navigation, and their overall satisfaction.
Gather data on the overall effectiveness of the site, in relation to the goals of each task.

scenes.title: 13. Step 4 — Analyze results

items.b: transfer handwritten notes to the computer
write reports while fresh in your mind
results of each test, problem areas, comments, survey feedback
find the problem areas
source of the problem: navigation, text, graphics…
specific task-oriented issues

lines: Step four: analyze results. Compile and summarize the data, transferring handwritten notes to the computer.
Write your reports while they're fresh in your mind.
Create a summary table showing the results of each test, with problem areas, comments, and survey feedback.
Identify difficulties and problem areas, and why they happened: specific factors like navigation, text or graphics.
And identify any specific task oriented issues.

scenes.title: 14. Step 5 — Make recommendations

nodes.b: gather all info → translate into recommendations
concentrate on high-level functionality
what works and what doesn't for users

lines: Step five: compile and recommend. Gather all the compiled information and translate it into recommendations.
Concentrate on high level functionality first.
Then focus on improving the user experience: what works, and what doesn't work well for users.
Determine the implementation plan, and write up a formal report.

scenes.title: 15. Best practices

items.b: early stage of design & development
before development — sets usability standards for your audience
experts, non-experts, or 50-50
poor connectivity audience → limit to e.g. 56 Kbps
focus on critical & frequently used functions
multiple testers per observer compromises results
teach devs: outcomes are a sign of improvement

lines: Best practices. The primary goal is to find crucial usability problems before the product is launched.
Start testing during the early stage of design and development.
Test your competitor's product before you begin development. It helps set usability standards for your target audience.
Select appropriate users: experts, non-experts, or a fifty fifty mix.
Use a bandwidth shaper. If your audience has poor connectivity, limit testers to something like fifty-six kilobits per second.
Concentrate on critical and frequently used functionality.
Assign a single observer to each tester. If one observer watches many testers, results may be compromised.
And teach designers and developers that test outcomes are not a sign of failure, but a sign of improvement.

scenes.title: 16. Pros & cons

items.b: uncovers usability issues before the product is marketed
improves end-user satisfaction
makes the system highly effective and efficient
from your real target audience — not “opinions” from random people
usability lab takes lots of resources · recruiting & managing testers is expensive

lines: Pros. It uncovers usability issues before the product is marketed.
It improves end user satisfaction.
It makes your system highly effective and efficient.
And it gathers true feedback from your real target audience, instead of opinions from random people.
The con is cost. Setting up a usability lab takes lots of resources, and recruiting and managing testers is expensive.

scenes.title: 17. User Acceptance Testing (UAT)

items.b: formal testing to determine whether a system satisfies its acceptance criteria, based on business requirements — lets functional users decide whether to accept the system
confirms the system is fit for purpose to business stakeholders
plan properly · start as early as possible · allow time to test and fix problems

lines: User acceptance testing, or U A T, is formal testing to determine whether a system satisfies its acceptance criteria, based on business requirements,
so that the functional users can decide whether or not to accept the system.
It's probably the most important test phase of all, because it confirms the system is fit for purpose for business stakeholders.
U A T must be planned properly, start as early as possible, and allow enough time to complete testing and fix any problems.

scenes.title: 18. Where does UAT fit in?

cells: User Acceptance Test (UAT testers, business users)

lines: Where does U A T fit in the software development life cycle? Requirements, written by business analysts, are verified by user acceptance testing, run by U A T testers and business users.
Functional specifications, from system analysts, are verified by the system test.
Technical specifications, from developers, are verified by unit tests.

scenes.title: 19. UAT and the V-model
lines: The V model. Down the left side: client needs, requirements, functional specifications, technical specifications.
Up the right side: unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and finally U A T.
Each test level checks the matching level on the left.
U A T sits at the very top, checking the system against the client's needs.

scenes.title: 20. UAT lifecycle

nodes.b: what to test · estimate time & effort · prepare test plan
document test scenarios · everything in place
run all tests twice: cycle 1 finds bugs, devs fix, cycle 2 retests
report findings → input to go-live decision

lines: The U A T lifecycle has four phases. Planning: identify what needs testing, estimate time and effort, and prepare the test plan.
Preparation: document the test scenarios, and make sure everything is in place to run the tests.
Execution: run all planned tests twice. The first cycle finds bugs, developers fix them, and the second cycle retests.
Completion: report what was found to the project team, as input to their go live decision.

scenes.title: 21. Test design process

nodes.b: from the test basis
from user stories
detailed scenarios
test estimates · test data requirements · resource estimates · test environment requirements

lines: The test design process. Gather information from the test basis.
Create high level test definitions, from user stories.
Prepare formal test scenarios.
These feed the U A T plan: test estimates, test data requirements, resource estimates, and test environment requirements.

scenes.title: 22. Good UAT tests…

items.b: based on user roles & business processes
a business user can easily understand them
specify data only where essential to the outcome
a different user will execute it slightly differently
expected results clearly described
verified by business users before execution starts

lines: Good user acceptance tests are based on the user roles and business processes needed to support the business.
They're written so that a business user can easily understand them.
They only specify the data to be used where it's essential to the outcome.
They're written so that a different user will execute the scenario slightly differently.
They clearly describe the expected results.
And they're verified by the business users before test execution starts.

scenes.title: 23. What is interface testing?

nodes.b: e.g. web server
APIs, web services — commands, messages & attributes that enable communication
e.g. application / database server

lines: Interface testing is done on the application under test, to verify that communication between two different software systems is done correctly.
A connection that integrates two components is called an interface. In computing it could be anything, like APIs or web services.
An interface is software made of commands, messages and other attributes that enable communication between a device and a user.

scenes.title: 24. What & why to test

items.b: proper error message for any query
outcome when web server connection resets midway
+ check user-friendliness of commonly used areas
verify security as communication propagates
handle failures between app server and website

lines: Interface testing covers two main segments: the web server to application server interface, and the application server to database server interface.
It checks that servers execute properly, that errors are handled with a proper error message for any query, and what happens when the connection to the web server resets midway.
Why do it? So end users don't hit problems, and to check the user friendliness of the areas they use most.
To verify security requirements as communication propagates between systems.
And to check the solution can handle network failures between the application server and the website.

scenes.title: 25. Types of interface testing

items.b: interface engine handles your standard workflows as expected
unexpected values — e.g. date, month and day reversed
high-volume interface may need more load testing than low-volume
each system alone — e.g. billing and inventory of a retail store work separately

lines: Types of interface testing. Workflow: the interface engine handles your standard workflows as expected.
Edge cases with unexpected values, like a date with the month and day reversed.
Performance, load and network testing: a high volume interface may need more load testing than a low volume one, depending on the engine and infrastructure.
And individual systems: test each system on its own. For a retail store, billing and inventory management should each work separately.

scenes.title: 26. Interface testing strategy

nodes.b: performs the implementation-neutral tests
instantiates the object, runs A-specific tests
instantiates the object, runs B-specific tests

lines: Strategy: to test an interface with common tests regardless of implementation, use an abstract test case, then create concrete instances for each implementation.
The base, or abstract, test case performs the implementation neutral tests,
while the concrete tests instantiate the object to test, and perform any implementation specific tests.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Quick recap.
Usability means effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction. Test with five steps: plan, find people, conduct, analyze, recommend.
U A T confirms the system is fit for purpose, and interface testing checks systems talk correctly. You've got this.
